newsitem.title: USA: U.S., EU to try to resolve differences on technology.
newsitem.headline: U.S., EU to try to resolve differences on technology.

text.p: U.S. and European Union trade chiefs were set to meet Thursday in an effort to resolve a dispute over information technology and move forward on the effort to get an international agreement.

Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky, who last week accused Europe of backing away from an agreement to eliminate tariffs on a wide range of electronic products, told reporters that she would discuss the technology accord with European Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan late Thursday.
She said she was encouraged by a letter this week from Brittan on the issue, but that Europe lacked unity on the matter which made it difficult to reach agreement.

"I am encouraged, but I don't think we're there yet," Barshefsky told reporters following a speech to a business group. "Clearly Europe has to come to a rapid decision on this issue. We will not be able to move forward on this initiative ... without Europe because we will not let Europe free ride on our tariff reductions."

The Information Technology Agreement (ITA) would eliminate tariffs on a wide range of information products including computer chips, software and telecommunications equipment. Barshefsky and Brittan were in Seattle to attend a meeting of Quadrilateral (Quad) trade ministers which also includes Canada's Arthur Eggleton and Japan's Shunpei Tsukahara.
Barshefsky has said that Quad leadership on a technology deal is needed to win a global agreement at the first meeting of World Trade Organisation ministers to be held in Singapore in December.

Barshefsky declined to discuss the content of the letter, but EU sources in Brussels said that Europe was backing down from an ultimatum that insisted on European inclusion in a U.S.-Japan semiconductor alliance in order to press for a wider ITA agreement.
The letter was said to suggest that work on the ITA could begin if the "discriminatory aspects" of a U.S.-Japan chip alliance, renewed this summer, were not applied until after the ITA is finalised.

But Barshefsky said the semiconductor issue can be easily resolved and that Europe appears to be backing away from the ITA because it does not have full agreement among its members. Brittan has denied that Europe is backing away from the ITA.

U.S. government and industry officials have said that some EU member states are seeking other trade concessions as a price for ending duties on information technology even though European electronic companies are willing to see tariffs dropped.

"There is no question that Europe is holding back on the ITA, using as an excuse the issue of semiconductors, which we think is readily resolveable, or using as an excuse the need to link ITA with other unrelated issues," Barshefsky said.
"It is clear there is at this point, no unanimity among the (EU) member states to move forward as aggressively as we, Canada, Japan and others are ready to move," she added.
